en: HSS 8 from NSUG Xc 14/39: Śākyarakṣita, *Hevajrābhisamayatilaka* (*Dpal kye rdo rje’i mngon par rtogs pa’i thig le*). Toh. no. 1277. Derge Tanjur, vol. TA, folios 105r.6–130r.6. Translated by Byang chub rtse mo and Skyob pa dpal bzang po.
Oṃ namaḥ śrīhevajrāya || Om. Homage to the glorious Hevajra.
Dancing amidst the sun situated upon the chest of his enemy who lies upon a radiant, universal lotus, he is blue, accompanied by his consort, holding a thunderbolt and a lotus in his two hands;
he possesses the six seals, wears a garland of severed heads, has deformed faces, three eyes, and tawny hair.
May he, the hero who seizes the three worlds and whose crown is marked by the universal vajra, remove your darkness.

In this regard, the yogi— having obtained his authority through ritual, being devoted to the guru, pure in livelihood, truthful in speech, and free from doubt— sits upon a comfortable seat marked with a universal vajra in some place conducive to the mind, such as a cremation ground or similar location, after having purified his mouth with the five nectars and other substances.

Having performed the protection of the place, oneself, and the yoga by means of the mantra *oṃ rakṣa 2 hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā*, one should visualize a blue syllable *hūṃ* situated upon a solar disc arising from a red lotus within the hollow of one’s own heart.

Having illuminated the interior with its five rays, one should draw forth the Blessed One, the Hero Śrī Trailokyākṣepa of the form to be described, as well as the venerable Guru, through the pores of every hair; having brought them forth and established them in the sky before one, one should worship them after prostrating, with external, secret, and essential (tattva) offerings originating from the seed-syllable in the heart.
Therein, the offering of the five types of worship, such as divine flowers and incense, is the outer worship (*bāhyapūjā*).

The offering of substances according to one’s own commitment (*svasamaya*) by means of the goddesses Gaurī and the others, who have been emanated from the seed-syllable, is the secret worship (*guhyapūjā*).

In that regard, in the eastern, southern, western, and northern directions of the Blessed One are Gaurī, Caurī, Vetālī, and Ghasmarī; they are black, madder-red, yellow, and dark-green in color, and they hold in their hands the bodhicitta in a skull-cup, the *svayambhū* flower, vajra-water, and medicinal herbs.

In the intermediate directions of Īśāna and Agni, the preeminent goddesses Pukkasī and Śavarī are blue and white in color, respectively, and hold in lotus vessels the essence of strength (*bala-rasa*). As for the statement in the *Dvikalpa* that "Pukkasī holds a vajra in her hand," there too it is explained as being [an offering of] vajra-meat.
In the southwest is Caṇḍālī, dark blue like the sky, playing a *kṛpīṭa* drum.
With these, Gaurī and the others, is performed the secret worship (*guhya-pūjā*).
In some explanations, the outer worship (*bāhyapūjā*) is described as being performed by Caṇḍālī holding a hand-drum (*ḍamaru*).

In the northwest is Ḍombī, of variegated color, embracing her own body; she, having merged with Nairātmyā, embraces [her] at the throat and performs the reality-worship (*tattvapūjā*) consisting of great bliss (*mahāsukha*). This is stated in the *Ekadevī*: "The other goddesses, having entered within the single goddess, perform the worship through great bliss. Because all [goddesses] possess identity due to being fashioned from the continuum of the yogin, the tradition (*āmnāya*) holds that even though they belong to different continua, their mental-form bodies (*manomayamūrti*), being beyond comparison, abide in one place—this is what is meant by "entering" (*antarbhāva*).
There is also a view held that when Nairātmyā has departed, Ḍombī embraces the neck of the Lord and worships him with the worship of reality consisting of great bliss (*mahāsukha*).

As for the claim that the secret worship is performed by the eight goddesses, while the worship of reality is the experience of non-dual bliss in a single flavor together with Nairātmyā—that is not correct, because it does not mention the activity of the gesture of embracing by Ḍombī. Furthermore, it is stated in the Tantra: "His neck embraced by Ḍombī through the passion of great desire."

Following that, having performed the sevenfold supreme worship—consisting of the confession of one’s own sins, the rejoicing in the merit of others, the entreaty for the Perfectly Awakened One to turn the Wheel of Dharma, the supplication for the Tathāgatas who desire to enter *nirvāṇa* to remain in *saṃsāra*, and the dedication of one’s own merit arising from [acts such as] increasing [virtue]—I go for refuge until reaching the seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) to the Buddha Śrī Herukavajra, whose nature is the Great Bliss encompassing the entire triple world; to the Dharma in the form of the mantras, mudrās, maṇḍalas, and so forth taught by him; and to the assembly of yoginīs situated within his wheel.

I generate the mind whose nature is great bliss, directed toward perfect enlightenment, which is characterized by emptiness endowed with the excellence of all aspects and serves as the cause for the welfare of all sentient beings.
I take refuge in the unsurpassed path to awakening, namely the Vajrayāna;
I offer myself to the host of vajra consorts, headed by the illustrious Hevajra.

Having performed the practices beginning with going for the three refuges and ending with the offering of one's own body, one should cultivate: loving-kindness (*maitrī*), which consists of the desire to unite all sentient beings with the great bliss of a single flavor, just like an only son; compassion (*karuṇā*), which takes the form of the wish to rescue those beings who are drowning in the ocean of conceptual construction and lack refuge; joy (*muditā*), whose nature is the desire for the separation [of beings] from the attachment to the enjoyments and sovereignty resulting from roots of merit that have arisen; and equanimity (*upekṣā*), characterized by a flow of delightful experience within the true nature (*dharmatā*) that is everywhere free from aversion and attraction. Having meditated upon these, [one should proceed].

Having recited "Oṃ, all phenomena are pure by nature; I am pure by nature," preceded by this visualization for the sake of increasing the yogi’s accumulation of wisdom—the accumulation of merit having already been acquired—one should meditate on the emptiness of all phenomena according to one's inclination through two methods, as taught by the guru.
Among these, this is the first method: one should resolve that the entire universe, the Blessed One, and his seat have entered into the clear light (*prabhāsvara*).

The second [method], however, is as follows: having caused the universe together with the goddesses of worship to enter the Blessed One [who resides] within the seed-syllable, one should dissolve oneself into the sun at one’s own heart; the sun into the syllable *hūṃ*; the *ū* into the *ha*; the *ha* into the head; the head into the half-moon; the half-moon into the bindu; and the bindu into the *nāda*. Having contemplated even that [nāda] as being a hundred-thousandth part of the tip of a hair, one should recite while internalizing the meaning: “Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the wisdom of emptiness,” and then abandon even that conceptualization. This is the Blessed Lady Prajñāpāramitā, whose nature is the non-apprehension of all phenomena.
Then, by the power of the impetus of former vows, he would arise from the samādhi of emptiness, which is naturally luminous by nature and like space.

In this regard, the sequence for emerging from meditative absorption (*vyutthāna*) is as follows: One should visualize in the sky a blue *hūṃ* syllable arising from the seed-syllable *raṃ*, which transforms into a crossed-vajra (*viśvavajra*) with three prongs, radiating five-colored rays of light. Through its rays, which are as unbearable as the fire at the end of an aeon, one should contemplate that it pervades all and then solidifies into a square, blazing vajra-fence extending as far as desired; above it, a vajra-canopy; below it, a vajra-curtain; and beneath that, a ground made of vajra reaching down to the very bottom of the earth (*ārasātala*).
And that enclosure wall and so forth should be understood as having the nature of pure mundane cognition, by virtue of its purity consisting in the removal of obstacles and the like.

Then, within the vajra-fence, one should visualize the great *dharmodayā*—triangular due to the purity of body, speech, and mind; white as the autumn moon because it is free from all obscurations; and vast because its nature is that of the Vajradhara who embodies the three bodies (*trikāya*). Because it shares the characteristics of a womb (*yoni*), it is narrow at the bottom and broad at the top. Within that, due to the purification of the eight consciousnesses, one visualizes the center of the eight cremation grounds. Due to the purification of the smearing of the eight worldly dharmas, there is the pericarp of a universal lotus born from the syllable *paṃ*, which is also characterized by selflessness.

Upon the heart of a corpse lying within the pure realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), there is a solar disc that betrays its power by eclipsing the splendor of the three worlds produced by its own radiance. Above that is the moon, which has the nature of the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) and is the essence of skillful means (*upāya*), transformed from the doubling of the vowels. Above that is the sun, which has the nature of the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*) and is the essence of wisdom (*prajñā*), transformed from the doubling of the consonants excluding *ḍa, ḍha, da, dha, ya, la*. Because of the boldness of wisdom, it is situated above [the moon], like a woman who takes the active role in lovemaking. One should contemplate their union as great bliss (*mahāsukha*).

Then, having meditated upon two blue seed-syllables, *hūṃ* and *aṃ*, consisting of wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*), situated within the union of the mother and father like the sun and moon, one should contemplate that very same pair of seed-syllables—situated upon the sun and moon within the interior of the curved knife (*kartī*) and vajra—which have arisen from their transformation and whose nature is the wisdom of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*).

Having performed the welfare of the world through the nets of their rays, having illuminated and summoned all the Tathāgatas, and having caused them to enter therein, one should contemplate the wisdom of accomplishment (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*) as the unification of them all.

Through the transformation of the seed-syllables and emblems of the moon and sun, one visualizes oneself as the glorious Trailokyākṣepanātha, whose nature is the wisdom of the perfectly pure dharmadhātu. He is blue through the purity of great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*); in some [traditions], he has a blue body because of hatred (*dveṣa*) for the destruction of the afflictions of conceptual construction. He is wrathful because he subdues the wicked;
he has one face through the purity of non-dual wisdom (*advayajñāna*).
He has a distorted face due to the abandonment of false views;
he is terrifying with prominent fangs due to the destruction of the four Māras;
and he possesses a loud laugh through the purity of his intent to crush pride.
He has three eyes through the purity of body, speech, and mind; or, through the purity of seeing all forms of the three times, or through compassion, he has red eyes.
He has brown hair standing erect because of his mastery over subduing the wicked; some say his hair is erect because he stands above the entire universe.
Some maintain that he has a crown marked with a *viśvavajra* (double-vajra) because he bestows grace upon the universe, and because he demonstrates the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
With his forehead adorned by five skulls through the purification of the five families,
and with two arms through the purification of the two accumulations; [he holds] a sword in his right hand for the purpose of shattering the mountain of ignorance, and because it is on the right side.
Through the purity of the state of equal flavor (*samarasībhāva*) of the five wisdoms, he holds a blue five-pronged vajra;

with his left hand—because the left side pertains to *prajñā*—he is intent on embracing [his consort], and through the purity of the blood of the four Māras and the purity of the essence of compassion, he holds a skull-cup marked by a vajra and filled with blood.
Through the purity of the two truths, he has two feet.

With the left foot placed upon the tip of the right foot— purified by the upward movement of the bodhicitta as the means, which purifies the indication of the supportlessness of the three realms, and which is like the sun upon the heart of the corpse sleeping on the universal lotus— and with the tips of his big toes slightly touching the seat, he stands in the dance posture of the half-lotus (*ardhaparyaṅka*), purified by his attachment to great compassion that is free from all anger and aversion.
Through the purification of the three bodies—the Dharma, Sambhoga, and Nirmāṇa—he is in the triple-bent posture (*tribhaṅga*);

through the purification of the fifty letters of the *āli* and *kāli*, his body is adorned with a fresh garland of fifty severed heads with entrails still attached; and through the purification of Akṣobhya, Amitābha, Ratnasaṃbhava, Vairocana, and Amoghasiddhi, he bears the five mudrās: a golden wheel on his head, earrings, a necklace, bracelets, and a girdle.

He bears the sixth mudrā by virtue of his entire body being smeared with smooth ashes made from bones purified as Vajrasattva, which indicates the pervasion of *bodhicitta* throughout all limbs; others say he has a body smeared with the ashes of the burnt world.

He wears a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) made of human hair due to the purity of non-conceptual Brahman, and he is clothed in a tiger skin representing the purification of passion and other afflictions through their transgression.

With her right hand, she holds a curved knife through the purity that severs the conceptual constructions of existence and non-existence; with her left, she holds a skull-cup filled with the pollen consisting of great bliss and great compassion.
She has one face, wears the five mudrās, and possesses a garland of fifteen dry heads representing the fifteen vowels through the purity of emptiness.

Some masters say that she has a forehead adorned with five skulls, a mass of tawny hair standing upright, three round red eyes, and a face made terrifying by the sprouts of her fangs; she wears a slipping girdle and, through the yoga of the "union of the casket" (*sampuṭayoga*) with Nairātmyā—who is dark blue like the syllable *Aṃ*—she experiences non-dual great bliss (*advayamahāsukha*), her entire body bristling with hair as her form is embraced by a *ḍombī*, her neck being encircled by her.

He possesses the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) because he delights in the playful enjoyment of his own consort who has transcended the three realms; the heroic sentiment (*vīra*) because he overcomes the three realms; the loathsome (*bībhatsa*) because he wears ornaments such as garlands of human skulls and because of his playfulness; the comic (*hāsya*) because of his dense, shimmering laughter that imitates the erotic; the furious (*raudra*) because of his fangs that mock the vast splendor of the fierce sun at the onset of cosmic dissolution; and the terrifying (*bhayānaka*) because his form causes terror in all gods and demons—even while his nature is the great bliss unmarked by any conceptual construction.

One should meditate [on the Buddha] as having great compassion because he accomplishes the welfare of the world according to their capacities through infinite series of emanations projected by the momentum of his former vows; as marvelous because he has transcended the world due to the extreme loftiness [of his realization]; and as peaceful because the mass of afflictions such as passion has been stilled and because he is without beginning or end.

As for the internal purity of the Blessed One: in the flesh is Pukkasi, in the blood Śabarī, in the semen Caṇḍālī, in the marrow and fat Ḍombī; the seven skins are, in order, the seven factors of enlightenment; and the bone is the four truths.

Thus, the yogi, possessing the ego-identity of the *samayasattva*, beholds the syllable *HŪṂ* within the vajra-fist situated upon the sun at the center of the Lord’s heart, and the syllable *AṂ* upon the moon held within the sheath of the curved knife (*karttikā*) born from the seed-syllable *AṂ* located on the moon within the heart of the Blessed Lady. Having first performed the radiation and reabsorption of its rays, he draws forth and brings the *jñānasattva*, establishes him in the sky before him, and worships him by first offering the guest-water (*argha*) and other offerings through the goddesses such as Gaurī, who have been projected by the rays of the seed-syllable in his own heart.

Having praised him, one should draw him in with the syllable *jaḥ*, cause him to enter like water into water for the sake of the empowerment of the *samayasattva* by means of the syllable *hūṃ*, bind him with the syllable *baṃ*, and satisfy him with the syllable *hoḥ*.
Immediately thereafter, having drawn in all the Buddhas who have been summoned by the hook-shaped rays from the seed-syllable in the heart, one should entreat them as before with the Eight Mothers:
"Just as the great festival was bestowed upon the Buddhas by Bodhivajra..."
For the sake of my protection as well, grant me the Sky-Vajra and the rest.
"Oṃ, may all the Tathāgatas consecrate me!
Thus, by those Buddhas in the form of Heruka,
he is consecrated with the Great Vajra, which is venerated by the three realms.
"I bestow [this] which arises from the treasury of the three secrets of all the Buddhas.

While reciting "Oṃ sarvatathāgatābhiṣeka-samaya-śriye hūṃ," [the disciple] is consecrated with the waters of wisdom contained in vases made of the five nectars and embodying the five Tathāgatas, with the intention of washing away all stains of the obscurations along with their latent tendencies.

At the very moment of the consecration, there occurs a rain of saffron and flowers accompanied by the sound of drums; one is worshipped by Rūpavajrā and the others, and praised with the vajra-songs of Locanā and the rest as they will be described. Because [the disciple] has arisen from the meditative absorption of the Lord of the Family through the purification of that worship, Akṣobhya arises upon the heads of the Blessed Lord and Blessed Lady from the remaining liquid of the consecration.
Then, while reciting "Oṃ sarvatathāgatābhiṣekasamayashriye hūṃ," one should consecrate the empowerment with the thought, "I am of the nature of the vajra."

Then, having donned armor upon the sense faculties without interruption: on the eyes is the white [deity] identical to Māyājvālāvajrī, who bears the name Mohavajrī; on the ears is the black [deity] identical to Nairātmyā, who bears the name Dveṣavajrī; on the nostrils is the yellow [deity] identical to Guhyagaurī, who bears the name Mātsaryavajrī.

In the mouth is Rāgavajrī, who is red and resembles the inner Yoginī of Water; in the body is Īrṣyāvajrī, also known as Vajraḍākinī, who is green; and in the mind is Nairātmyayoginī, who is black, like the one named Nairātmyā.

These should also be visualized as arising from the seed-syllables *āṃ*, *āṃ*, *aiṃ*, *aiṃ*, *auṃ*, and *giṃ* respectively; they have one face and three eyes, hold a curved knife and a skull-cup in their right and left hands, and sit upon a moon resting on a corpse. Furthermore, at the crown, throat, and heart, [one should visualize] *oṃ*, *āḥ*, and *hūṃ*.

One should visualize her as having a white, red, and black complexion, born from the syllable *hūṃ*, and as the *Caryā*, *Khecarī*, and *Nairātmyā* who have emerged from the three worlds. Some say she is born from the seed-syllables *oṃ āṃ āṃ*. As for her shape, it is like that of Mohavajrā and the others. Likewise, first, according to the sequence of Saroruhavajra:

The *Jñānasattva-āveśa* (invocation of the wisdom-being), the empowerment, and the sequence of the armor are clearly perceived. In the *Abhisamaya* of Lūyipa’s tradition, the sequence is as follows: the *jñānasattva* is invoked immediately after the armor, and then the empowerment is conferred. Likewise, this has been written in the *Sādhana of the Two-Armed Hevajra* following the intention of Śāntipa.

To state that one is consecrated after having recited the armor-mantra without interruption—until the wisdom-maṇḍala has been placed within the treasury of complete purity—is not in accordance with the intention of the two Siddhas. Immediately following that, in front [of oneself], from a blue syllable *jaṃ* arises a wind-maṇḍala in the shape of a bow, marked by two fluttering banners at its two tips.

Above that, from a red RAṂ, arises a triangular fire maṇḍala marked with three corners by the letter REPHA. Above that, resting upon a tripod formed by three heads, is a skull-cup (*kapāla*), the vessel of a lotus, arisen from a red letter Ā. In its center, from the complete transformation of BHRŪṂ ĀḤ KHAṂ HŪṂ, [arises] gokudahanī.

The five lamps of the intrinsic nature of *bīraśuma* and the five nectars are consecrated by their respective seed-syllables; above them, one visualizes a white *oṃ*, from which arises the pervasive form of the syllable *āṃ*.

Above that moon mandala, one should visualize a white syllable *hūṃ* from which arises a vajra marked with its seed-syllable. Then, by fire fanned by the wind, all those circles of vajras and the vajra itself melt; having been processed within that very vessel of nectar produced from the melting of the four sets of five, they are refined.

Then, one should visualize it as being filled with that very [essence]. Having visualized the three syllables Oṃ Āḥ Hūṃ upon it, their light rays—in the form of circling firebrands—invite the nectar residing in the three realms of existence and the wisdom-nectar of all the Tathāgatas. These are then introduced into that very [essence], whereby they become of equal taste.

Having visualized [the nectar] as stainless as the light of the autumn moon, possessing divine fragrance and flavor, one should visualize at the tip of one's own tongue a vajra the size of a grain of rice arising from a white HŪṂ. Then, with its light rays like a whirling firebrand, one causes the Blessed One to partake of that nectar and offers it into the mouth of the Blessed Mother.

*oṃ sarvatathāgatasvabhāvavajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham*. By reciting this, the Blessed One was pleased. Then, from the seed-syllable at his heart, Vajrarūpā and the others emerged, holding a mirror, a lute, a conch for perfumes, a vessel for tastes, and various garments.

One should perform worship continuously with the hands of Dharmadhātu, reciting: *oṃ sarvatathāgatapūjāvajrasvabhāvātmako ’haṃ*. Then, with Locanā and the others: "You are completely surrounded by the assembly of yoginīs; you have attained the supreme realization of your own mind."

"You have adorned all beings, both moving and unmoving; with a heart of compassion, you awaken sentient beings. O Heruka, whose mind accomplishes the vajra of illusion and conceptual elaboration—Glorious Vajra, may your mind rejoice! Thus one should praise with this vajra song, and then recite: *oṃ sarvatathāgata-stuti-vajrasvabhāvātmako ’haṃ*.
Thereafter, one should form the mudrā that is the nature of the four wheels; therein, the red navel-wheel is situated below the navel.

Alternatively, upon the center of a multicolored lotus with sixty-four petals radiating light, one should empower the black syllable *āṃ* facing upward. Upon the navel is a white Dharma wheel with eight petals; in its center is the blue seed-syllable *hūṃ*, and on the petals in the directions starting from the east...

The seed-syllables of Vairocana and the others are, respectively, BHRŪṂ, ĀḤ, JRĪṂ, and KHAṂ. On the petals in the northeast and the other directions are the seed-syllables of Locanā and the others—ĀE, VAṂ, MĀ, and YĀ—which are situated below these [syllables]. At the throat is the saṃbhoga-cakra, a red lotus with sixteen petals.

Its tongue is a red syllable *āṃ*, completely encircled by the *ālikāli*, with its opening facing upward. At the crown of the head is the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*), a thirty-two-petaled lotus, empowered by a white syllable *haṃ* at its center, facing downward. All of these syllables rest upon moons.

Then, having performed the benefit of beings by emitting masses of light rays from those four wheels into the sky, one should meditate upon that very [reality] within. Following that, in order to constitute the portions of the five families, one should place *oṃ*, *hūṃ*, *svā*, *āḥ*, and *hā* respectively upon the crown, heart, navel, secret place, and the two thighs of the Bhagavatī.

From the complete transformation [of the seed-syllables], one should visualize Vairocana, Akṣobhya, Ratnasambhava, Amitābha, and Amoghasiddhi. From the complete transformation of *hūṃ*, one should visualize a lotus and a vajra; and from the syllables *āḥ* and *oṃ*, one should visualize a full-blown bud and a jewel.

Then, having performed the consecration of the lotus and the vajra with: *oṃ padmasukhadhārama hārāgasukhandacaturānandabhagaviśva hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ kāryaṃ kuru śvame | oṃ vajramahādveṣa caturānandadāyaka khagamukha ākaraso nātha hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ kāryaṃ kuru śvame ||* ...by means of these [mantras], one should perform the consecration of the lotus and the vajra.
In order to attain the primordial wisdom of great bliss without emission, one should visualize the yellow syllables HŪṂ and PHAṬ within the cavities of the lotus and the vajra.

Then, reciting the three syllables of *śrī*, one should perform the act of passion with this: *oṃ sarvatathāgatānurāgaṇavajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham*. One should also mentally attend to all [practices], such as entering into meditative union (*samāpatti*) with the action seal (*karmamudrā*) regarding the commitments (*samaya*), and the accomplishment of that which possesses the components of the five families.

Furthermore, a yogi who is conceited regarding impure bliss should accomplish that. Then, at the time of the empowerment of the wisdom-knowledge (*prajñājñāna*), through the distinctions of characteristics such as the various aspects realized from the oral instructions of the sublime guru, and likewise through the power of familiarity with the meditative union of the action-seal (*karmamudrā*)—such as joy and so forth—at the end of their gradual arising, [the ultimate state is reached].

The sequence is as follows: one is firmly established in the luminosity that is free from the web of all conceptual constructions, which is the fourth [joy], the innate bliss that abides momentarily in all gateways, possessing aspects that are not characterized by stains. Alternatively, the sequence therein is as follows: the three worlds are the charnel ground; the charnel ground is the lotus seat; the lotus is the corpse; and the corpse is the sun.

The Sun [deity] makes a request to the Bhagavatī out of devotion to the Bhagavatī; [the request is made] to the Bhagavat at the heart of the Bhagavat, to the Sun [deity], to Vajrasūrya, to that which abides at the hub of his vajra, to the letter *hūṃ* which is the essence of Amoghasiddhi, to the letter *ā* within that *hūṃ*, and to the letter *ha* which is the nature of Amitābha.

Upon the head of the syllable *Ha*, renowned as Ratnasambhava, which is the nature of Vairocana; upon the half-moon, which is the nature of Candracchaṭā (the Moon-Flake), which is the nature of Vajrasattva; and upon the drop (*bindu*), which is the essence of Akṣobhya—one should cause [the deity] to abide within the *nāda*. According to some, the drop is the nature of Akṣobhya.

Thus he spoke on the nature of Vajrasattva. Furthermore, with a mere superior intelligence, one should contemplate even the *nāda* as being no more than a hundred-thousandth part of the tip of a hair and then discard it; that very state, which is the supreme emptiness of existence and non-existence and so forth, is like a cloudless sky—luminous and radiant—and is just as it was before.

One should view it exactly as such through the power of accomplishment, which abides by the force of one's aspiration. Likewise, having engaged in the activity of arising again and again, the yogin should then repeatedly enter into the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*), just as the breath-wind that abides in the mirror pervades everywhere.

This stage is the yoga that directly realizes the nature of the inseparable two truths, the resultant Vajradhara, which is the nature of neither duality nor non-duality. This is the method for entering the luminosity (*prabhāsvara*) through meditation on reality (*tattva*) together with wisdom (*prajñā*). In contrast, this is in comparison to meditation devoid of wisdom.

For it is said: "The very face of pure wisdom is *tvam-ga* itself; O Wisdom, you who have entered *tvam-ga*. Therefore, the arising of the coemergent through the yoga of *caṇḍālī* and so forth is the thorough entry into luminosity (*prabhāsvara*). In that regard, first, as for the yoga of *caṇḍālī* here: within the clear form of the deity, there is either the syllable *āṃ* itself at the navel wheel, or...

As a cause for stabilizing the mind, having completely withdrawn the two descending life-winds and caused them to enter the *avadhūti*, the fierce fire ignited by the wind below the navel—straight, extremely subtle, and in the form of a slender flame—blazes as the Blessed Lady Caṇḍālī, who bears the name of the Supreme Nairātmyā.

The five Tathāgatas residing in the heart-cakra and the four goddesses, Locanā and so forth, are incinerated; this continues until one touches that which is not "delightful" (amanorama) residing in the crown-cakra. Likewise, while the blazing Bhagavān Moon is dripping [downward], at that time, Caṇḍālī is made to blaze rapidly.

That [fire] blazes intensely and the moon (the one with the hare) flows very swiftly; having become unified with the *caṇḍālī* while focusing on the navel-maṇḍala, the mind becomes firmly fixed. Furthermore, as the bodhicitta flows forth and is accumulated in the emanation-wheel (*nirmāṇacakra*) and the others, it is gathered there.

Through the sequence of supreme joy, from the crown of the head down to the lotus and the tip of the vajra-jewel, emptiness and compassion—inseparable and uninterrupted—gradually increase; having reached this state, one is thoroughly purified by the light of the *caṇḍālī* fire.

It pervades the thirty-two channels of the wheel of great bliss (mahāsukha-cakra), and from there it completely permeates the entire body as far as the seventy-two thousand other channels. By the power of the great bliss of the separation from joy—the internal sun and moon, the union of wisdom (prajñā) and method (upāya)—the aggregates, elements, and so forth, together with the Māras, [are overcome].

"112b3 'All these have become manifest and fully arisen' means that through the yoga of Caṇḍālī, one abides in clear light (*prabhāsvara*). This itself is the Dharma-mudrā; this itself is the application of the *bindu* of spring. Thus, 'spring' refers to the Blessed One, the Moon."

Its *bindu* is the Blessed Lady Caṇḍālī; "their union" refers to the union with this very [Caṇḍālī]. By means of the yogi who constantly practices Caṇḍālī and guards it steadfastly, the innate Caṇḍālī—having become the cause of supreme great bliss—should be made manifest.

Furthermore, the yogi who dwells in the vajra-like samādhi as neither dual nor non-dual realizes the supreme siddhi of Mahāmudrā. Regarding the term "yoginī," some proclaim it to be the realization of the Great Secret. Her path is to be clarified through the ten stages (*bhūmi*) via either the wisdom-mudrā (*jñānamudrā*) or the dharma-mudrā (*dharmamudrā*).

Later, he is taught as a Vajradhara. In some cases, through the application of the action seal (karmamudrā)—one who has arisen from the family of the vajra and so forth, resides in [the appropriate place], and possesses the capacity to attain primordial wisdom—one enjoys and unites with her for one month and so on; thereby, the nature of great bliss and compassion expands infinitely and is not obstructed.

Having directly realized the samādhi of emptiness—the coemergent great bliss endowed with the seven limbs—one will enter the supreme state. Within one month, the Great Vajradhara, whose body performs the purpose of entering the meditative transitions (*sandhyā*) as a collection of emanations that delight in the clusters and ornaments of the assembly of qualities, shall bestow [this].

Alternatively, having practiced the *vidyāvrata* for six or seven months, and having transformed oneself into the form of the deity, when one is able to constantly incline toward the yoga of reality—just as day and night are joined together by an intensely blazing radiance—at that time:

Together with the mudrā, one who possesses the yoga of Hevajra should initiate the effort of meditative union during the morning, the transitional periods, and so forth, in order to practice the innate (*sahaja*).

The stage of yoga is the state of being perpetually established, day and night, like the appearances and the further increase of appearances through the power of the great bliss of equal taste, which is sealed by the vajra-mudrā; it is the nature of the unity of all three realms of existence, which is both universally uniform and yet the singular essence of that which is not universally uniform, and is thus utterly liberated.

Then, at the end of the stage of supreme joy (*pramuditā*), when the dawn breaks, the practitioner will directly realize the reality (*tattva*) of the fourth joy and achieve the supreme accomplishment (*uttamasiddhi*). Furthermore, in the *Guhyasamāja*: "The application of all means for what is to be accomplished, through which it becomes manifest—joining the vajra and the lotus is called the near-accomplishment (*upāsādhana*)."

"Endowed with the syllables HŪṂ and PHAṬ, it is proclaimed as the accomplishment of movement; its nature is the peace of one's own bliss—this shall be described as the great accomplishment. Thus, through these four branches of method, [it reveals] the means for the state of the glorious Great Vajradhara and the Great Vajradharī, and the qualities of all the Buddhas.

By the phrase "the dharma to be relied upon," this very [process] is intended as the sequence for its direct realization. If one enters into meditative equipoise with the action seal (*karmamudrā*), then, because of becoming one-pointed, the rabbit-possessor (the moon) is melted by that previously mentioned, intensely blazing fire of *caṇḍālī*; through the power of the innate (*sahaja*), [the result arises].

Their yoga is to be described as the yoga of the fierce heat (*caṇḍālī*) of action, accompanied by wisdom (*prajñā*). For one without a consort (*prajñā*), it is described as the meditation on the form of the deity or all internal meditations; through the constant blazing of the fierce heat itself, the innate (*sahaja*) arises.

Furthermore, at the time of initiation (*abhiṣeka*), the blazing that arises from entering into union with an external consort is the *caṇḍālī* of this [practice]. Just as before, its arising from the dawning of the innate (*sahaja*) is held to be the yoga of the *karmacaṇḍālī*. Nevertheless, it is said: "It is indeed the innate, yet it does not follow after the beauty of her face."

Therefore, this yoga of the fierce heat of karma is certainly not for the face alone. Nevertheless, some do not again achieve mastery over breath through the conquest of the winds and practice as before, nor [do they achieve it] at the immeasurable navel mandala on the path of the winds.

Alternatively, this great bliss arising from the blazing of that *caṇḍālī* through grasping is taught as the yoga of the *karmacaṇḍālī*. If one wishes to stabilize the mind through the yoga of the *bindu* and cause the manifestation of all accomplishments (*siddhi*) to expand, [then...]

At that time, having visualized the four syllables such as ĀṂ at the apertures of the channels of the navel and other cakras, the wind residing in the secret cakra perfectly stirs the fire; by the light rays of the blazing syllable ĀṂ, which is the nature of *caṇḍālī*, the three syllables such as HŪṂ completely melt.

One should meditate on [the drop] as having the nature of innate joy, inseparable from the syllable *oṃ*, in the form of a bindu. When the meditation is complete, one should cause it to radiate; from that, one should visualize the subtle *tattva* remaining like a single, blazing mass of radiant rays.
Filled with the nectar melted by its light, it becomes a radiating drop; that too becomes a white ray of light, and one should gaze until the mind reaches that drop.

One should proceed as follows: furthermore, the sign of attaining stability is perceived for a duration. Through that perception and stability, one clearly sees various lamps radiating from the lattice-work of light rays, appearing with a brilliant glow; and one sees everything like a myrobalan fruit in the palm of the hand.

The "expansion of the appearance of all meditative concentrations" refers to the yoga of the *bindu*. Alternatively, one should place within that *hūṃ* syllable—which is in the form of a *bindu*—the three worlds summoned by the Tathāgatas emanated from the mass of light rays of the mantra at the heart; this should be done for as long as the mind desires.

Following that, through the stages of the path of joy, one reaches the culmination of the vajras of body, speech, and mind. Having gathered [all things] together by means of the light rays of those [vajras] in the manner of inhaling the breath, one swiftly enters the seed-syllable drop (*bīja-bindu*), which is the maṇḍala of that Blessed One as it has been described. Regarding the meditation on the wheel, one should cause the maṇḍala-wheel to enter.

Once again, by means of the manner of joyful exertion, light rays radiate forth, illuminating the world; having merged with those very [rays], one should meditate for as long as desired upon the Tathāgatas—who are performing the benefit of beings—entering the heart in the manner of drawing in the breath. This is the yoga of the supreme bindu.

Alternatively, one should visualize that the light rays of the *samādhisattva* enter the *avadhūti*, melt the bodhicitta abiding in the circle of great bliss (*mahāsukha-cakra*), and [return] from that very place to abide in the form of subtle atoms identical in nature with the *bindu* of the syllable *HŪṂ* at the heart; this is the *binduyoga* according to others.

Following that, the cultivation of the subtle yoga is the supreme method for settling the mind. In that very way, the letters such as *āṃ* and so forth melt into a single taste; through the nature of the coemergent, they become the bodhicitta-tilaka, the size of a mustard seed, endowed with the clearly manifest body of the Blessed One.

114b1 Regarding the visualization of the mandala circle: one should visualize the mandala circle at the tip of the vajra-jewel. From there, it descends and rests upon a lotus, or else one should visualize it resting at the tip of the nose. Having seen the signs of stable abiding as they were described, 114b2...

"Bhagavān, one should meditate on its mandala or emanate the mandala"—this refers to the subtle yoga. Having meditated upon that very [mandala] in the form of the deity, one should, through the yogas of uninterrupted recitation or by means of other yogas as appropriate, enter into, arise from, and meditate upon the clear light (prabhāsvara).

When weariness arises, one should recite the mantra according to this ritual procedure, or otherwise utter the syllables of the mantra. In that regard, those light rays emerging from the mouth of Prajñā enter one’s own mouth, exit through the path of the vajra, and enter the lotus of the goddess; then they again emerge from the mouth of the goddess and enter one’s own mouth.

"One should cause the stream of mantra to remain uninterrupted"—thus it is stated in the *Saroruha-sādhana* regarding recitation with the "palanquin" (*khyogs*). Otherwise, through the pride of the equality of all phenomena, the mantra garland enters one’s own mouth; from the vajra path, it emerges into the lotus, and from the path of the *avadhūti*, it issues forth from the mouth of the Bhagavatī.

"One should recite while meditating that [the syllable] enters exactly as it is through the opening of one's own mouth and revolves [therein]"—this refers to what is called "recitation with a relaxed and peaceful syllable" performed by means of a carriage (khyogs). This very same [syllable], having entered the mouth of the Bhagavatī and returning through one's own mouth, becomes firm and harsh due to the specific distinction of this movement; this is the "wrathful recitation."

It is the wrathful recitation because it expresses the heart-mantra and so forth with supreme intensity. Alternatively, one should visualize a garland of mantra syllables residing at the *hūṃ* syllable located in the heart, circling it like a row of lamps; then, having abandoned inferior realizations, one should recite while visualizing it as rapidly revolving.
oṃ trèlokyākṣepa hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā | Of the Blessed One...

This is the root mantra. Furthermore, its three *hūṃ* syllables are taught as being short in the second tantra (*Dvikalpa*) and its commentary. Then, having offered the *bali* that will be explained below and also made aspiration prayers, one should remain at ease. When it becomes the time for the session break, one should arise from the form of the Blessed One and perform the insertion of the wisdom-being (*jñānasattva*) and so forth.

At the conclusion of the midnight session, having performed everything [as before], one should go to sleep with the firm conviction that sleep is of the nature of luminosity (*prabhāsvara*). At the conclusion of the dawn session, one should be awakened by the vajra songs of the four goddesses, Locanā and the others, and perform all activities such as rising. Then, the mantra for moving the city is:

oṃ āḥ ka ca ṭa ta pa ya śa svāhā | Regarding this, the oral instruction is as follows: having visualized oneself in the form of Hevajra together with Prajñā swiftly, one should imagine an eight-petaled red lotus at his heart; then, on the petals in the eastern and other directions, one should arrange the syllables *ā ka ca ṭa* in clockwise order according to the proper sequence.

In the intermediate petals, such as those of Īśāna (northeast) and so forth, are the syllables *tapayaśa*. In the central pericarp, there is *svā* in the east, *oṃ* in the center, and *hā* in the west; all of these reside upon sun mandalas and are red in color. Furthermore, light rays from these, in the form of iron hooks, emerge from the pores of the skin.

Having summoned the object of accomplishment and placed it beneath the feet of the practitioner, one should recite the mantra while contemplating, "I shall bring these very ones under my control. By reciting it one hundred thousand times, the city will be moved. For the purpose of the practice of subjugation, one should first perform one hundred thousand recitations for the sake of the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) according to the stated sequence.

Having performed the gaṇacakra in a charnel ground, since the practitioners of the gaṇa also desire to slay the practitioner who seeks [the goal], one should therefore seize the skull. Then, having gone to a certain location...

Placing the head toward the east, one should lie on a high pillow; having touched the sole of the foot with a skull-cup filled with *māmaki*, one should recite [the mantra] once. When rising later, having drunk all of that, one should again recite [the mantra] once while focusing the mind upon the entire location of the wheel of the *dhāraṇī*.

The yogin who has no doubt regarding Hevajra should perform purification in every respect. Then, according to the sequence of the Kālacakra, the recitation of the *ālikāli* should be performed. By means of the sounds of *akacaṭatapayaśa*, the *ālikāli* is expressed through their implicit meaning: OṂ A Ā | AI ĀI | RI RĪ | AU ĀU | LI LĪ | AA ĀA | AE ĀEE |
Recite "a ā aṃ aḥ a o au aṃ āḥ ha hā ya yā ra rā va vā la lā" according to the sequence of emanation while inhaling; this is the recitation of the *āli*.

Ka Kha Khā Ga Ghā Gha Ghā Ṅa Ṅā Tsā Tsā Tshā Tshā Dzā Dzā Dzhā Dzhā Ñya Ñyā; Ta Tā THa THā Da Dā Dha Dhā Na Nā; Ta Tā Tha Thā Da Dā Dha Dhā Na Nā; Pa Pā Pha Phā Ba Bā Bha Bhā Ma Mā; Da Dā Dha Dhā Na Nā; Sa Sā Ṇya Ṇyā Śha Śhā Ṭhka Ṭhkā Svā Hā. Thus one recites the *kāli* while the breath flows out.

By reciting the *āḥ ali k’a li* one hundred thousand times, the mantra practitioner who causes the three worlds to arise should make [the object] the size of one [finger], and then again the size of one; this bestows summoning, protection, and enrichment. This sequence is also seen in the *Śrīvajragarbha-prakaraṇa*.

Then, as for the pith instruction on subjugation: one quickly visualizes oneself as the form of Heruka together with Prajñā, upon a beautiful heap of red lotuses; at the heart, [one visualizes] the pericarp of a sixteen-petaled half-red lotus.

From the syllables ĀṂ and HŪṂ—which are the essence of the perfect synthesis of A’A LI and KHA KI and which are thoroughly attached to the qualities of a Buddha—and through their being intensely visualized in the mind, masses of extremely powerful and delightful rays of light definitely radiate forth, illuminating all wandering beings.

Having summoned the bodies and minds of others, one should cause those very syllables ĀṂ and HŪṂ to enter their respective drops (*bindu*). Then, through their complete transformation, they become bees in the form of Kuruvindeśvara, intoxicated by drinking the honey of supreme compassion.

He is one whose mind is thus [concentrated]. By means of the sound of the extremely long syllable *hūṃ* uttered by him, one should visualize oneself in the form of Nairātmyā and Heruka; and within their respective hearts, one should clearly generate minute syllables *āṃ* and *hūṃ* upon a bindu the size of a mustard seed, resembling [the color] dyed with vermilion.

Then, that *manas* (mind), mounted upon the chariot of the exhaled breath, emerges through the nostrils; having purified and sustained the body, speech, and mind of sentient beings, it mounts the inhaled breath once more and is made to enter the pericarp of the heart-lotus by way of that very same path.

Then, one should cause the body, speech, and mind that have been summoned from all directions to dissolve into one’s own body, speech, and mind through meditative concentration (*samādhi*). In this manner, one should meditate again and again, generating [the visualization] until it becomes clearly manifest.

Thereafter, one should visualize a red eight-petaled lotus that has reached the heart of the object of accomplishment (sādhya) or the female object of accomplishment (sādhya-strī). With that very "mind-churning" (*manmatha*) bee, [the object] is summoned and made to enter the lotus at the heart—which is the nature of the body, speech, and mind—within the nostrils of that [object]. Then, that mind-churning bee, by means of the pollen which is the nature of her body, turns oneself into a reddish-yellow color.

Having drunk the honey of the nature of speech and consumed the flower of the mind, one then draws that mind with the breath-wind of the practitioner; having drawn it out through the nostrils of the object of accomplishment, one inserts it into the lotus at the heart of the practitioner. Then, with the wings, one shakes off the dust from the flower of that person's body.

One should visualize the honey of speech and the flower of mind as being vomited forth. In this manner, one should repeatedly and intensely cultivate passion; at the conclusion of the meditation, one should recite the mantra that increases the non-existence of the object to be accomplished. By means of these, there is the branch of vidyā which causes those who are intoxicated by joy.

Having first performed an ablution to bring oneself under control, one should practice meditation; for if one perceives the defects in human desires at that time, it will become a defect of non-perception. Therefore, from the very beginning, [one should distinguish between] the sublime and the non-sublime.

One should meditate after having analyzed the objects of the senses. This is the sequence for subduing the mind through the "bee" [meditation]. Regarding the rituals for the fire offering (*homa*) and so forth in the activities of pacification and the rest, they are well known from following the tantras and other sources, and thus have not been written here. The *sādhana* of the two-armed Hevajra who delights in the charnel ground is as follows:

Once again, having performed everything as before, one should visualize a blue syllable *hrīḥ* upon a moon disc at the heart; from that syllable *hrīḥ* situated within a moon disc at the center of a vajra, all of which has completely transformed, one should meditate on the Blessed One himself alone, possessing the form previously described, standing in a dancing posture upon a half-moon resting on a corpse.

Clad in human skin; the remainder is as before. The mantra to be recited is: *śrī heruka vajrasamaya hrīḥ | sarvaduṣṭān mudrāprabhañjaka hūṃ phaṭ*. This too was spoken by the Blessed One in the *Saṃpuṭatilaka-tantra*.

Thus, with reference to the meditator, the *sādhana* of the Blessed One alone—distinct from the condensed and luminous [deity] together with the *vidyā*—has been explained. Furthermore, its extensive clarity is as follows: within the *vajrapañjara*, there is a triangular *dharmodaya*, white like the autumn moon due to the abandonment of all obscurations, and [shaped] by the purity of body, speech, and mind.

Because it is the nature of the vajra itself, wherein the three bodies are one ground, and because it is the great source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*), one should meditate on it as being narrow below and wide above. Within that, in the center of the eight charnel grounds, from a blue syllable *hrīḥ* abiding upon the union of moon and sun, there arises a vajra; within its hub, upon a moon disc, is the syllable *hrīḥ*.

"Having visualized the blue syllable" refers to the extensive [practice]. Within the beautiful source of phenomena (dharmodaya), upon a multicolored lotus situated inside, in the center of a perimeter of crossed vajras (viśvavajra), there arise from the syllables YAṂ, RAṂ, BAṂ, and LAṂ [four goddesses] of blue, red, white, and yellow complexion. Their two principal faces have the shape of a bow and are marked with a bow.

Its three corners are marked by tridents; it is circular and marked by a vase; its four sides are marked by three-pointed vajras. From the complete transformation of the four great elements—the natures of wind, fire, water, and earth—there arises a tiered palace composed of various precious gems, which is the essence that perfectly encompasses the buddha-fields and is purified by Vairocana together with Prajñā.

The four-sided celestial mansion, which is the very nature of the non-duality of the Tathāgata and ordinary beings, has four gates in the east and other directions; these are the purity of the applications of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of miraculous power, and the faculties. The gates themselves are the very means of awakening.

The eight pillars at the eight doorposts represent the purity of the eightfold noble path; they are the pillars that bring near the qualities of all Buddhas. Because the burden of benefiting others has already been taken up through the purity of the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), there are four beams above the pillars. These are [the bodhisattvas] Śūraṅgama, Gaganagañja, Vimalamudrā, and...

The four pedestals, firm and beautiful, are purified by the four *siṃhavikrīḍita* (Lion’s Sport) samādhis. The individual sides are purified by the dhāraṇīs of patience, phenomena, meaning, and mantras; that is, the patience for the knowledge of phenomena regarding each truth, the knowledge of phenomena, and the patience for the subsequent knowledge of phenomena.

Due to the purity of the momentary distinctions of the characteristic of the knowledge of subsequent realization, two goddesses abide in each of the two sides of the root gates in clockwise order: Vīṇā, Vaṃśā, Murajā, Mṛdaṅgā, Paṭahā, Mālā, Lāsyā, Gītā, and Nṛtyā.

The sixteen goddesses—Puṣpā (Flower), Dhūpā (Incense), Dīpā (Lamp), Gandhā (Perfume), Ādarśā (Mirror), Rasā (Taste), Sparśā (Touch), and Dharmā (Dharma)—are yellow, red, white, smoke-colored, yellow, red, reddish-pink, multicolored, and white.
The black, golden-hued, yellow, white, red, green, and white-complexioned goddesses possess forms corresponding to their respective names and are born from their respective initial syllables.

The eight vases filled with nectar represent the complete purity of the nectar of the accumulations of merit and wisdom, which are moistened by compassion and vast; they correspond to the sūtras that follow from the power of intention, as well as the melodic narrations (*geya*), prophecies (*vyākaraṇa*), verses (*gāthā*), solemn utterances (*udāna*), and introductory accounts (*nidāna*).

It was adorned with banners moved by the wind, which possessed the sound of bells, and through which the pure, all-pervading sound of the sublime Dharma—renowned as the twelve branches consisting of *avadāna*, *itivṛttaka*, *jātaka*, *vaipulya*, *adbhutadharma*, and *upadeśa*—resounded everywhere.

They are like the *chattra* because they pacify the pervasive torment of wandering in saṃsāra through their application according to reality, or because they have abandoned all conceptual constructions; and they are like the *bhadraghaṭa* and the *kalpavṛkṣa* because they accomplish the excellence of the welfare of others through such things as the various jewels of diverse merit.

Because it purifies the root afflictions, the supramundane path of meditation is the necklace (*hāra*); because it completely removes the afflictions, the mundane path of meditation is the half-necklace (*arddhahāra*); because the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*) is purified, it is the moon; because wisdom and gnosis (*prajñājñāna*) are purified, it is the sun.

The fly-whisk represents the purity of the Tathāgata’s wisdom of the path; the flower garland represents the purity of the excellence of the flowers of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*); and the mirror represents the purity of mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*). Thus, it is also stated in the *Sarvamaṇḍala-guhyamahātantra*: "The necklace is correctly explained as that which definitively destroys all afflictions."
It robs away the afflictions, completely cuts them off, and utterly destroys them.

118a1 || It is that which utterly subdues and completely clears away; it is the application of the two accumulations. Because it steals away half of the afflictions, it is called the "half-necklace. The bodhicitta, which is naturally luminous and pure, is unsurpassed. Because it accomplishes the welfare of all sentient beings, it is called the "moon mandala. Wisdom and gnosis are pure by nature.

The vajra-like samādhi has arisen; it is the great majesty of the world of liberation. The solar mandala shall be described: it is the wisdom of samādhi that is definitively liberated from the two types of conceptualization. The excellence of the wisdom of the path is correctly explained as the *cāmara* (fly-whisk); likewise, the seven factors of enlightenment are like a garland of hanging flower-clusters. Thus it is said.

The teaching of the Dharma as appropriate for those with subtle, coarse, or middling intellects, and for those lacking certainty, is purified by being unguarded, thus it is the unguarded red garland of *bakula* flowers. The teaching of the supremely white supramundane Dharma is purified by [the four truths], thus it is the *kramaśīrṣa*. The four archways are purified by the four meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*).

Because it cuts through the discordant factors for teaching the Dharma, it is the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*). Its spokes are eightfold: on one side, [the truths of] suffering (*duḥkha*), origin (*samudaya*), cessation (*nirodha*), and the path (*mārga*); and [the categories of] the conventional (*saṃvṛti*), the ultimate (*paramārtha*), the mundane (*laukika*), and the supramundane (*lokottara*). According to another system, there are twelve; [the spokes] should be known as *duḥkha*, [and so forth]. It is known.

It is not to be known again; origination is to be abandoned; it has been abandoned; it is not to be abandoned again. Cessation is to be realized; it has been realized; it is not to be realized again. The path is to be cultivated; it has been cultivated; it is not to be cultivated again. Thus, he turned the wheel of Dharma in twelve aspects, which is perfectly pure.

It is the purity of the twelve links of dependent origination. Through the grace of relying upon the perfectly pure Dharma of valid authority spoken by the Blessed One, [one overcomes] the mountain of evil non-Buddhists...

The male and female deer who follow the Dharma and faith apply themselves to the path; being pure through their application to what is called the Wheel of Dharma, these male and female deer possess throats that are free from fear. Through purity of moral shame (*hrī*), they possess canopies, garments, garlands, and so forth.

Because they are entirely free from individual fetters, they turn the wheel of Dharma according to the vajra-method of all the perfectly enlightened Buddhas; because their vajra-garlands are pure, they blaze with rays of light; and because Vairocana and the others are pure, they possess the colors of the earth and so forth.

The others have not been written here because they are already well known. Thus, having visualized the multi-storied palace (*kūṭāgāra*), one should visualize oneself as the Blessed One in its center, according to the sequence beginning with the variegated lotus (*viśvapaṭma*) as before; [this is] the *oṃ āḥ* which is the nature of body, speech, and mind.

The three syllables, *hūṃ*, enclosed between two red *ho* syllables, known as the intermediate state being (*antarābhava-sattva*), enter through the mouth of the Blessed One with universal joy; passing through the vajra-path, they enter the lotus of the goddess and melt within her womb. Finally, the Blessed One also melts together with his consort due to intense passion.

By means of the form of the bodhicitta, which is like quicksilver, one abides in the nature of great bliss. Then, without interruption, the yoginīs such as Pukkasi and the others—who are of the nature of great loving-kindness and so forth—become deeply distressed in their minds, thinking, "We are without a protector! [They pray: "O Venerable One, arouse the mind of compassion!"

Pukkasī, protect me! Abandon this very nature of emptiness and grant me great bliss! Since I shall die if you are not present, O Hevajra, please arise! Abandon this very nature of emptiness and grant me success as a mountain-dweller! O Lord of Joy, seeker of the world’s hospitality, have you entered into emptiness?
"Since we do not know the direction where you are, we, the outcaste women, offer this petition.

We understand your intention; O noble lady, our mindfulness has failed us. Do not let your stream of compassion cease, but arise, O Mistress of Miracles! Thus were they exhorted by those who sang the vajra songs, and by the power of their former aspirations, she was awakened by the mere sound of the vajra songs.

Arising like one waking from a dream, he then proceeds in the petals of the directions—east and so forth—in their proper sequence: Brahmā, Indra, Yama, and Rudra; and in the petals of the intermediate directions, such as the northeast, [he places] Kṛtānta, Nirṛti, and Rākṣasa.

In the hearts of the Viśvabhū [Buddhas], upon a moon disc situated on a moon and sun in union, according to the ritual procedure, there arise from eight drops of the bodhicitta emanated from the Blessed One the syllables GAṂ, CAṂ, BAṂ, GHAṂ, PAṂ, ŚAṂ, LAṂ, and DAṂ; from these, there arise a curved knife, a staff, a tortoise, a snake, and...

Having visualized the letters that are non-different from [the deity] and which always abide upon the moon—[namely] the lion, the monk, the wheel, and the vajra—and through the sequence of awakening at the source of the five elements, all of these completely transform into the eight yoginīs, such as Gaurī and the others, possessing their respective colors, forms, and feelings, as they have been described.

He has the nature of the aggregates of perception and mental formations, as well as the elements of earth, water, fire, and wind; he is single-faced, possesses three round, red eyes, and has two arms. In his right hand, he holds a curved knife (*kartṛkā*), a *caṅte'u*, a tortoise, a snake, a lion, a monk, a wheel, and a vajra.

It is the cutting off of conceptualizations such as [the notion of] entities and so forth; it is the cutting off of the scriptures, envy, hatred, pride, the thought of awakening, and ignorance; and it is the virtuous manifestation of primordial wisdom (*jñāna*). To the left are Rohitā and the sow.

The skull-cup, the yogic bowl, the battle-axe, the mendicant’s staff, the plowshare, and the threatening gesture; these sever the mass of ignorance, emptiness, attachment, and so forth, serve as reminders for these [practices], and eradicate obstacles.

This is the miraculous manifestation of the purity of the single-dharma essence. She dwells in the hearts of Brahmā and others upon lunar discs in the posture of the half-lotus dance; she holds the five mudrās, wears a garland of fresh heads, has a contorted face, and her orange-red hair streams upward.

One should meditate on them as being clothed in the directions. Within the hearts of all [the deities], one should visualize their respective seed-syllables resting upon moons, which themselves rest upon their respective hand-symbols; having first performed the activity of emanating and reabsorbing through conditions, thereafter, by means of the light rays from the seed-syllable at the heart, the wisdom-mandala is summoned and emanated by the *gaurī*.

Summon with *oṃ gaurī ākarṣaya jaḥ*. Insert with *oṃ caurī praveśaya hūṃ*. Bind with *oṃ vetālī bandhaya vaṃ*. Subjugate with *oṃ ghasmarī toṣaya hoḥ*. Then, at the conclusion of the empowerment, [offer to] Gaurī and the others who reside upon the petals of the directions, beginning with Akṣobhya.

[The seals] of Vairocana, Ratnasambhava, and Amitābha [are established]. Furthermore, for Pukkasī and the others, the purification of the mudrās of Akṣobhya and the rest, following the sequence of Gaurī and the others, is as described in the *Dvikalpa* (Hevajra Tantra). Thereafter, all the armor and so forth are exactly as before.

Regarding the tasting of the nectar (*amṛta*): according to the ritual procedure, one should offer it to the Blessed One himself with one's own wisdom (*prajñā*). As for the members of the retinue, such as Gaurī and the others, they should taste it through the application of the tongue-vajra (*jihvā-vajra*). Furthermore, in this context, the "pavilion" (*kūṭāgāra*) is to be understood through examination. The empowerment is Akṣobhya, the Tathāgata; the tasting of the nectar is Amitābha; and the praise is Ratnasambhava.

The worship that brings about the accomplishment of the meaningful is correctly explained; having always visualized the one who is attached as Vajrasattva, these six branches of accomplishment (siddhi) shall be described. These should also be understood in relation to the three maṇḍalas that will be explained hereafter. As for the entry into clear light: in a single moment, the three worlds [become] charnel grounds within charnel grounds.

In the case of the multi-storied houses (*khang pa brtsegs pa*), [the mantras] are in the nostrils of the Bhagavān in each respective direction, such as Gaurī and the others; the remainder is as before. Then, the mantras that become those of Nairātmyā and the others are as follows: *oṃ āṃ svāhā* is the heart mantra of Nairātmyā; *oṃ līṃ svāhā*.

*Gaurī*: Oṃ Āḥ Svāhā. *Caurī*: Oṃ Aiṃ Svāhā. *Vetālī*: Oṃ Auṃ Svāhā. *Ghasmarī*, who performs all activities: Oṃ Aḥ Svāhā. *Pukkasī*: Oṃ Raṃ Svāhā. *Śavarī*: Oṃ Laṃ Svāhā. *Caṇḍālī*: Oṃ Laṃ Svāhā. At this point, whenever one wishes to perform the recitation of the samaya-mantra for any [of these goddesses], [one should do so].

When the heart mantra and the near-heart mantra, which will be explained, are recited from the seed-syllable at the heart, the assembly of deities of the mandala is perfectly emanated. Having performed the benefit of sentient beings, they are summoned back together with the mantras in the manner of a rosary; at the time of the inhalation of the breath, they should be made to enter that very seed-syllable at the heart.

When the individual recitation of the mantras of the goddesses is completed, one should emanate and reabsorb them one by one; this is the mantra recitation of the samaya. Furthermore, as stated in the *Dvikalpa*: Vajrī, Gaurī, Varuṇī, Vajraḍākinī, Nairātmyā, and Khecarī.

Since it is stated that "the practitioner of the yoginī-observance (*vratin*) performs [rites] such as the immobilization (*stambhana) through the practice of the *cāmuṇḍī-yoga*," here too, following the oral instruction on the inseparable union with the Guru, the extensive ritual procedure shall be written: from the seed-syllable *ĀṂ*, there arises a yellow Vajrī.

Visualizing a yellow seed-syllable *hūṃ* at the heart of one who holds a skull-cup and a *khaṭvāṅga* in the left hands and a vajra and a curved knife (*kartṛ*) in the right hands, one should perform the fire offering according to the ritual procedure using the mantra—including the expansion formulas that will be explained—after having completed one hundred thousand preliminary recitations (*puraścaraṇa*) with the mantra *oṃ hūṃ svāhā*.

Furthermore, for this [rite], at the conclusion of the activity, one should write the vidyā-mantra—*oṃ hūṃ vajre amukaṃ stambhaya hūṃ svāhā*—upon two unbaked clay bowls containing a circular water-maṇḍala marked by a yellow *thod le kor* (a skull-cup) and a vase, with a double-vajra (*viśvavajra*) resting upon it; then, fill one of them with ashes from a charnel ground.

Having joined two other earthenware bowls together, one should draw upon them the mandala of Mahendra marked with vajras in the cardinal directions; placing this beneath the ground, one should remain in the samādhi of pressing down with the left foot if a woman is the object, or the right foot if a man is the object, and then recite the mantra. By reciting it one thousand times, the target will be paralyzed.

From *aiṃ*, one visualizes a perfected white woman with the color of saffron, holding a noose, a *khaṭvāṅga*, a hook, and a vajra, and possessing a red seed-syllable *āṃ* at her heart. Having first performed one hundred thousand recitations of the service mantra *oṃ āṃ svāhā*, one should perform the fire offering according to the ritual procedure using the mantra together with the *speli-chig*. Furthermore, at the conclusion of this activity:

Visualize the object of accomplishment as red with disheveled hair, his neck bound with a noose; having been drawn in through the opening of his private parts with an iron hook, he falls beneath one's feet. Then, visualize a red syllable ĀṂ at his private parts from which fire blazes and fiercely flares up. For a male [object], it is exactly the same, but [the fire] is at the heart.

By reciting *oṃ āṃ gū rī ā mukhi me vaśamānaya svāhā*, one will certainly bring them under control. Visualizing a blue water-maiden born from the seed-syllable *aiṃ*, holding a skull-cup, a mallet, a vajra, and making the threatening gesture (*tarjanī*), with a blue syllable *khaṃ* situated upon a sun disk at her heart, [one recites] *oṃ khaṃ svāhā* one hundred thousand times.

Having performed the recitation, one should perform the fire offering (homa) with the mantra accompanied by the intercalated phrases as prescribed. Furthermore, at the conclusion of this ritual activity, one should visualize the victim with disheveled hair, suppressed, standing upon the wind, mounted on a blue she-mule, facing south, and being struck with a club in a state of rage.

Reciting: *oṃ khaṃ pāriyogena amukaṃ oṣṭhataya khaṃ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*, one will expel [the obstacle] within seven nights. Then, having visualized a blue syllable *jhrīṃ* situated upon a sun disk at the heart of a Vajraḍākinī born from the syllable *au*, who is like a river, one should recite: *oṃ jhrāṃ svāhā* one hundred and twenty-one thousand times.

One should perform the fire offering (homa) in accordance with the specific activity using the mantra accompanied by the ritual words. Furthermore, the final procedure for this activity is as follows: one should visualize the objects to be accomplished mounted on horses and donkeys, engaged in verbal dispute with their opponents. [The mantra is: OṂ JRIṂ VAJRA-DĀKINĪ [Name] and [Name] VIDVEṢAṂ KURU SVĀHĀ.

By reciting "DZRĪṂ HŪṂ HŪṂ HŪṂ PHAṬ SVĀHĀ," one causes [the enemy] to become utterly terrified. One should visualize the blue Nairātmyā, born from the seed-syllable ĀṂ, possessing a transformed form and holding a skull-cup, a khaṭvāṅga, a vajra, and a curved knife; at her heart, upon a sun disk, one should contemplate a blue syllable BUṂ. Then, one should recite "OṂ BUṂ SVĀHĀ" one hundred thousand times.

One should perform the fire offering according to the ritual procedure with the mantra accompanied by the ritual words. Furthermore, at the conclusion of this rite, one should draw a six-pointed wheel upon a brahmin skull using poison, lac, and blood from the ring finger; it should be marked with *hūṃ* at each of the points, and in the center: *oṃ bhuṃ nairṛtyāmuṣya jvaraya bhuṃ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.

Having written [the name] while increasing all forms of harm or affliction, one should recite it and burn it in a fire of chaff; thus, one causes the onset of pestilence. Having visualized a Khecarī born from ĀṂ, white in appearance, with a red seed-syllable *hūṃ* at her heart, one should perform one hundred thousand recitations of *oṃ hūṃ svāhā*.

One should perform the fire offering according to the ritual procedure with the mantra accompanied by the appropriate words. Furthermore, for this activity, one should visualize the object of the rite upon a wind and fire mandala.

Visualizing them as blazing, one should imagine that the light rays from the seed-syllable at one’s own heart issue forth like iron hooks; they pass precisely through the left nostril and enter the right nostril of those to be accomplished. They pierce their hearts and birth-cavities, emerge from their left nostrils, and enter one’s own right nostril to be absorbed into the seed-syllable at one’s heart, being drawn in by the breath-wind.

By reciting *oṃ hūṃ khe tsari āmukīnā ākarṣaya hūṃ svāhā*, one performs the summoning. One should visualize the Earth-Dweller Nairātmyā, born from the syllable *āṃ* and resembling [the central deity], with a blue syllable *ghuḥ* at her heart; thus: *āṃ ghuḥ svāhā*. Having performed one hundred thousand recitations of this service (*sevā*), one should perform the fire offering (*homa*) as before, using the mantra together with the expansion phrases.

Furthermore, regarding this ritual action: one should visualize a blazing vajra arising from the syllable *ghuḥ* piercing from below the feet up to the waist of the victim. By reciting *oṃ ghuḥ bhucari amukam māraya ghuḥ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*, one effects killing. Here, according to the sequence of mantras taught in the Tantra, the Earth-Walkers (*bhūcaryaḥ*) and Sky-Walkers (*khecaryaḥ*) have transcended their respective stages.

"These seven, beginning with Vajrī, also abide in the *lalita* posture upon the sun and the letter *ra*; they have four arms, are adorned with the five mudrās, and have red hair streaming upward. Then, the heart mantras for Vajrī and the others are as follows: Oṃ āṃ svāhā; Oṃ īṃ svāhā; Oṃ ūṃ svāhā; Oṃ aiṃ svāhā.

oṃ āḥ svāhā | oṃ āḥ svāhā | Since the manner in which [the mandala] is condensed becomes clear in relation to the extensive version, this sādhana for the one possessing the maṇḍala is taught specifically for the two-armed form. Likewise, it should be understood that this applies to the four-armed forms and so forth as well.

The distinction between these is as follows: Jvalājvalāni is four-armed because she is pure through her definitive victory over the four Māras; with her primary right and left hands, she holds a vajra and a skull-cup filled with the blood of the Māras; and with her two remaining hands, she embraces Vajravārāhī, who is identical to Nairātmyā.

The embrace is as before. Its mantra is: OṂ JVALA JVALA BHYO HŪṂ HŪṂ HŪṂ PHAṬ SVĀHĀ. For this one as well, the three HŪṂ syllables are explained as being short. KITI KITI VAJRA refers to the three faces—representing emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), or the purity of the three channels—the first face being black and the right face white.

The left [hands] are red. He has six arms because he is purified by the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*). With his primary right hand he holds a vajra; with the left, a trident that destroys the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the three realms; with another, a curved knife (*kartṛkā*); and with the remaining one, he holds a bell (*ghaṇṭā*) that is purified by the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

With his remaining two hands, he embraces the Vajra-Chain (Vajra-lug-rgyud-ma), who resembles Nairātmyā, abiding as before. It is taught that the retinue is present in all [the deities]. Their mantra is: OṂ KITI KITI VAJRA HŪṂ HŪṂ HŪṂ PHAṬ SVĀHĀ. The three syllables HŪṂ are recited in the long [protracted] form.

Furthermore, Piṭhu-vajra arises from the syllable HŪṂ; he stands upon a sun disk situated within a skull cup born from the syllable HŪṂ. He has eight faces, purified by the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*). His central face is black, the right is white, and the left is red and extremely terrifying; his upper face is smoke-colored and fiercely contorted.

The remaining [deities] have the color of bees; each face has three eyes. With sixteen arms, purified by the sixteen emptinesses, the eight right hands hold, from top to bottom in sequence: phlegm, breath, madness, exhaustion (which is emaciation), leprosy, elephantiasis, and the spleen.

By means of the purity that overcomes the diseases of the swellings, [he holds] elephants, horses, donkeys, oxen, camels, humans, and *śarabhas*. Likewise, by means of the purity that bestows upon all sentient beings the sovereign accomplishments (*aiśvarya*) such as pacification (*śānti*), clarity (*prakaṭa*), and so forth, from the skull-cups situated in his left hands, [he holds] earth, water, wind, fire, moon, sun, Yama, and wealth.

The lords. With his two primary hands, he embraces Nairātmyā; with four feet, purified through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*); and as the cause for the complete conquest of the Māras of the aggregates, the afflictions, the son of the gods, and death—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śakra.

Some say that the four feet of the Great Lords (Maheśvaras) possess a playful grace, performing a dance with two feet in the half-lotus posture (*ardhaparyaṅka*) upon the sun at their hearts, while others perform a dance with the right leg extended. The ritual for the retinue is as before. The entry into the Clear Light (*prabhāsvara*) is as follows:

Through this classification, the eight yoginīs, such as Gaurī and the rest, are assigned to the eight faces; the seven faces are on the root face. The fourteen hands, together with their symbols, are on the two root hands; the two feet are on the two root feet. The inclusion of the variegated lotus and so forth is as before; it is the same as in other [texts].

Its heart mantra is: oṃ devapicu vajra hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. Here too, the three *hūṃ* syllables are said to be long. oṃ vajrakartari he vajrāya hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. This is the near-heart; it shall be known as the near-heart for all of these. oṃ āṣṭanāya piṅgorhva keśavartmane.

*Catuḥṣaṣṭinetrāya śodhaya bhujagāya kṛṣṇajīmūtabapuṣe kapālamālādhāriṇe ādhmātakrūracittāya ardhendudaṃṣṭriṇe māraya māraya kārāya kārāya gardzaya gardzaya tarjaya śoṣaya śoṣaya saptaśāgarān bandha bandha!*

*Nāgāṣṭakāna | gṛhṇa gṛhṇa | śatruṃ | hā hā hi hī hu hū he hee ho hoo haṃ haḥ phaṭ svāhā*. This is the mantra of the rosary. Furthermore, it is said that here, even from the mere distinction of the *adhiṣṭhāna-citta* (the supreme mind) within the central *Vajra*, Hevajra is seen as fourfold.

The uninterrupted sequence consists of the vast yellow vajra pavilion born from *bhrūṃ*, [representing] suffering (*duḥkha*), origin (*samudaya*), cessation (*nirodha*), the path (*mārga*), exhaustion (*kṣaya*), non-arising (*anutpāda*), phenomena (*dharma*), and subsequent realization (*anvaya*).

Through the purification of the ten cognitions—conventional knowledge and the knowledge of complete origination—one visualizes a blue syllable *hūṃ* situated in the center of the union of the moon and sun, which rests upon a variegated lotus and sun disk atop a variegated vajra with ten spokes located in the midst of saṃsāra; then, one proceeds through the stages of manifest enlightenment (*abhisambodhi*) as the source of the five elements.

From the complete transformation of all those [syllables], there arises [the deity] with a single face and the color of a blue sapphire, wearing a jeweled crown, with hands holding a vajra and a bell, embracing his natural consort from all sides, and treading upon Bhairava and Kālarātri with his left leg extended.

Having visualized oneself as Vajrahūṃkāra, adorned with variegated garments and ornaments, one emanates the ten wrathful deities through the application of the vajra-skull union; among them, in the spokes of the east and so forth, in successive order, are Yamāntaka, Prajñāntaka, Padmāntaka, and Vighnāntaka.

He is black, white, red, and blue in color, holding a vajra-hammer, a white staff, a red lotus, and a crossed vajra. He is short in stature with a large belly, wrathful, and adorned by the eight great nāgas. His orange-red hair streams upward, and he has three round, red eyes. [He is embraced] by Vairocana and...

They wear the crowns of Ratnasambhava, Amitābha, and Akṣobhya, and they hold tiger-skin lower garments. On the spokes beginning with the southeast, there are Kāmarāja, Nīladaṇḍa, Mahābala, and Acala, who are intensely black and hold a hook, a staff, and a trident.
