[They are] those who hold swords (123a7). Here, Kāmeśvara and Acala are adorned with fine garments, jewels, and so forth, and are graceful; they wear jeweled crowns. Nīladaṇḍa and Mahābala are distorted in appearance, like Yamāntaka. Below...

On the spoke [to the south] is Kṛtānta, black in color, holding a pestle and wearing a jewel crown marked by Akṣobhya. On the upper spoke is Uṣṇīṣa, yellow in color, holding a wheel and wearing a jewel crown marked by Vairocana. The four [deities] beginning with Kāmarāja wear crowns of Akṣobhya.

These ten wrathful deities are to be visualized as standing upon variegated lotuses and sun disks with their left legs extended, holding nāga-nooses with their left hands in fists making the threatening gesture at the region of their hearts. Having thus meditated upon the protective wheel (*rakṣācakra*), from the complete transformation of Vajra-Hūṃkāra in its center—

Having visualized the source of phenomena (dharmodaya) as having form, as previously described, one should likewise regard the four forms of Hevajra—possessing the variegated lotus, the variegated vajra, the celestial mansion (kūṭāgāra), and so forth—in accordance with the sequence taught in all other [tantras].

When, through the yoga of continuously and uninterruptedly meditating upon the generation stage within the mandala circles in such a manner, it becomes even clearer than clear, then, by means of the signs of the reflected images, it becomes non-conceptual and all-pervasive, like an illusion and so forth.

Thus, it is also stated in the *Dvikalpa*: "Through the yoga of the generation stage, the practitioner with vows cultivates elaboration. Having rendered elaboration like a dream, he makes that very elaboration non-elaborate. Just as a magical illusion, a dream, and the intermediate state [are empty], so too, through constant cultivation, the yogi perceives the mandala itself."

Therefore, it is said that one should immediately worship the Blessed One with whatever offerings are available, for the sake of increasing the yogi’s accumulation of merit through other meditations and for the purpose of pacifying obstacles—[the Blessed One] who is the Lord of the Ten Bhūmis, whose nature is the non-duality of the two truths, the Great Vajradhara, the Subduer of Māra. Thus he is worshipped.

The ritual procedure for that shall now be described. At dawn, the mantra practitioner endowed with the yoga of Hevajra should perform the sweeping and other preliminary tasks as appropriate for the location. Having touched the ground with his hand while reciting *oṃ rakṣa rakṣa hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ svāhā*, he consecrates the site. There, he should smear it with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), fragrant scents, and so forth.

According to their respective locations, they are designated as the *pīṭha* and *upapīṭha*, the *kṣetra* and *upakṣetra*, the *chandoha* and *upachandoha*, the *melāpaka* and *upamelāpaka*, the *śmaśāna* and *upaśmaśāna*. Having constructed a square *maṇḍala*, [one should proceed].

With "oṃ vajrarekhe hūṃ," one consecrates the perimeter. With "oṃ surekhe sarvatathāgatādhiṣṭhānena tiṣṭhantu svāhā," one should place a single flower in the center of the maṇḍala. Then, by means of light rays from the seed-syllable at the heart, one invites the Blessed One Trailokyavikramin, the Hero, surrounded by the eight goddesses.

Having first presented incomparable offerings such as arghya and so forth, one should first offer a single flower to the Bhagavat with the mantra: *oṃ āḥ hūṃ he vajraya vajrapuṣpe hūṃ svāhā*, using flowers and other items produced from the syllable *hūṃ* and consecrated by the three syllables. Thereafter, [one offers] with the heart and near-heart mantras: *oṃ āḥ*.

Having made offerings with "Nairātmyāyā vajrapuṣpe āṃ hūṃ svāhā," one should offer with the mantras: "Oṃ āṃ hūṃ svāhā" and "Oṃ a ā ai 124a6 ai au au ṛ ṝ lī lī ae aai ao au āṃ svāhā. On the crowns of both [deities], one should say: "Oṃ āḥ akṣobhyāya vajrapuṣpe hūṃ hūṃ svāhā."

On the petals in the directions of the east and so forth: *oṃ āḥ gaurī vajrapuṣpe gaṃ hūṃ svāhā*; *oṃ gaurī hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. With these, one should worship Gaurī. In that manner, one should perform the special worship of Gaurī and the others by interposing their respective seed-syllables with the three syllables.
Subsequently, having offered it together with the syllable *oṃ* and words of invocation, [ending] with the syllables *hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ* and concluding with *svāhā*.

One should perform the worship with flowers. Thus, having inserted the respective names such as *dhūpa* and so forth into the place of "flower" (*puṣpa*), one should offer them: then, *oṃ sarvatathāgatasurativallabhanirmite namo bhagavate śrīherukāya jjaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ pratīccha māṃ kusumāñjalirnātha*.

Saying "Hoḥ," one should bow after offering flowers with cupped hands: *Oṃ sarvatathāgatapūjāmeghaprasarasamudra sphara hīmaṃ gagana khaṃ hūṃ samanta svāhā*. This is the consecration of the offerings. Then: "The body whose nature is miraculous manifestation, The inseparability of emptiness and compassion, Completely vanquishing the illusions of Māra."

Having prostrated with the words, "I bow to you, O Hevajra," one should perform the confession of sins and so forth as far as one is able, and then recite: "May I be born into the [Buddha] family and possess the samaya; may I be free from delusion and teach Hevajra; may I be devoted to the Guru and endowed with compassion—may this be so in birth after birth. With hands holding the vajra and ringing the bell, may I read the profound Dharma."

"May the queen’s seed and my food arise and continue to arise in birth after birth. Having made this aspiration, he then recites the hundred-syllable mantra in order to restore any deficiencies or excesses in the ritual procedure: *oṃ vajrasattva samayam anupālaya | vajrasattva tvenopatiṣṭha | dṛḍho me bhava | sutoṣyo me bhava | anurakto me bhava | supoṣyo me bhava |*

Grant me all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhi*). May all activities (*sarvakarma*) be successful for me. Make my mind supreme (*cittam śreyaḥ*). Hūṃ ha ha ha ha ho! Bhagavān sarvatathāgatavajramāme muñca vajrī bhava mahāsamayasattva āḥ! And: Oṃ! You have accomplished every benefit for sentient beings; now grant the corresponding attainments (*siddhi*). Having departed for the realm of the Buddhas...

I pray that you return once more. *Oṃ vajra muḥ*—with these words, request them to depart. In this same manner, one should likewise proceed for the maṇḍalas of the four-armed, six-armed, and sixteen-armed [Vajravārāhī]. First, having made offerings with the three syllables, one should then offer with their respective mantras. For Vajravārāhī as well, one should present the offering with Nairātmyā.
As for the sixteen-armed [form], one should also perform worship with the eight-line offering mantra.

Oṃ āśīna-nāya hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā | Oṃ pidhor-dhvakeśa-pārśvane hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā | Oṃ caturviṃśatī-netrāya hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā | Oṃ ṣoḍaśabhujāya hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā | Oṃ kṛṣṇajīmūta-bapuṣe hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā |

Having performed the worship with the mantras: *oṃ ka pāla mālanekadhāri ne huṃ huṃ huṃ phaṭ svāhā*, *oṃ ādhmātakrūracittāya huṃ huṃ huṃ phaṭ svāhā*, and *oṃ ārdracandradamṣṭriṇe huṃ huṃ huṃ phaṭ svāhā*, one should perform the aspiration prayers and so forth as before, and then request [the deities] to depart.

Next, the ritual for the consumption of food shall be described. Regarding the food, soup, and so forth at the *gaṇacakra*, one should sprinkle them with nectar—prepared according to the ritual rules—with the ring finger of the left hand. Then, from the center of the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*), the wisdom circle (*jñānamaṇḍala*) is invited by means of light rays from the seed-syllable at the heart.

Alternatively, emanating from the seed-syllable at the heart, one should offer the previously mentioned mantras, augmented with the names of the substances of the food. Thereafter, requesting them to depart and slightly purifying the mouth with the samaya substances, one should present the bali offering according to the ritual procedure that will be explained.

When food is digested and passes down after being touched by the fire in the hearth of the navel, it should satisfy the *samayasattva* residing at the heart and the *samādhisattva*—or the syllable *Āṃ* wreathed in flames residing on the pericarp of the navel lotus—by dissolving into them; this is the procedure for the inner self-homa of external substances.

Then, having offered the remainder torma with "Oṃ autsaḥiṣṭha vajra ādhitiṣṭha ai maṃ baliṃ | gṛhṇa gṛhṇa hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ," one should discard the food. Regarding the inner fire offering (*antar-homa*) which is independent of external things: as before, it is ignited by the wind, [dispelling] all darkness and obscurations of conceptualization.

In the hearth of the navel mandala, one should perform the fire offering by burning with the extremely fierce Caṇḍālī and making offerings of the food of bodhicitta, [thereby] becoming the master of wisdom and method.

It is filled with the intense radiance of the sun and moon, which have become equal in taste. This second [offering] is also the unsurpassed fire-sacrifice (*homa*) that constitutes the worldly stage of exaltation; it is attained through moment-by-moment cultivation. Now, the *bali* offering shall be described: perfume, flowers, and so forth are placed to the right, and *śāka-ta* in front.

In vessels such as those made of *bhārala* wood, one should place fish, *jambūdikā* fruits, and other excellent foods, along with three ladles of water. Having also arranged whatever samaya substances have been obtained, one should set them out; then, observing them as before, one should transform them into nectar through the sequential ritual for tasting nectar (*amṛtāsvādana*).

One should visualize an eight-petaled red lotus situated within the hollows of the three—white, red, and black—which are the source of the phenomena of the three suchnesses, facing upward from top to bottom. Then, from the seed syllable at the heart, one emanates Gaurī and summons her with the mantra: *oṃ gaurī aindri ādityā saparivārā ākarṣaya jaḥ*.

Reciting *Oṃ tsauri indrā āditya saparivārāṇa praveśaya hūṃ*, they are inserted into the *tsauri* and lotuses. Reciting *Oṃ betālī indrā āditya saparivārāṇa bandhaya baṃ*, they are bound by the emanation of the *betālī*. Reciting *Oṃ ghasmarī indrā āditya saparivārāṇa praveśaya hoḥ*, they are brought under control.

On the central petal of the lotus situated at the center of that source of phenomena (dharmodaya), first is Indra, white in color, possessing a thousand eyes, with two hands holding a vajra and making the threatening gesture (tarjanī-mudrā), mounted upon a white elephant, the son of Airāvata. On the southern petal is Yama, black in color, with two hands holding a staff and making the threatening gesture, mounted upon a buffalo.

On the western petal is white Varuṇa, mounted upon a makara, possessing seven raised hoods of serpents, and holding a noose and a conch shell. On the northern petal is yellow Kubera, with a stout body, dwelling among treasures, and holding a *bījapūra* fruit and a mongoose in his hands. All of them are adorned with jewel ornaments and jeweled crowns.
Yama has a sun seat and sun-like radiance; in the northeastern petal is Īśvara.

The great white [deity] has three eyes, wears a crown of matted locks, and holds the mudrās of the trident and the skull-cup. He is clad in a lower garment of tiger skin, rides upon a bull, embraces Gaurī, and possesses a lunar seat and radiance. In the south-eastern petal is the fire deity, who is extremely red, has a protruding belly, and rides upon a goat.

He has eyebrows and matted locks that are reddish-yellow; his hands hold a rosary and a *kundikā* water-pot; he stands upon a solar seat and possesses radiance. On the petal in the direction of Nairṛti is the lord of the *rākṣasas*, blue in color, mounted upon a corpse, with reddish-yellow hair bristling upward and furrowed brows; he holds a curved knife and a skull-cup, while some say he holds a sword and a shield.

In the southwest petal is the blue Wind God (Vāyu), holding a wind-wheel; he rides upon a deer, wears a jeweled crown, possesses a moon seat and radiance, and is adorned with precious ornaments. At the pericarp is the yellow Earth Goddess (Pṛthivīdevī), adorned with precious garments and ornaments, holding a vase in her left hand.

To the right is the one who has previously made his vow, whose hands are joined in salutation; he dwells upon a moon-seat with moonlight, surrounded by hungry ghosts and darkness. Above him, on the eastern petal of the lotus of the source of phenomena (dharmodayā), resides [the deity] seated upon a white moon and a night-lily chariot drawn by white horses.

Holding with both hands a *kumuda* lotus marked by a moon, he has a moon seat and radiance. To the south is Sūrya, holding a lotus marked by a sun; he stands upon a green horse-drawn chariot and possesses his own seat and radiance. On the petals in the west and so forth, as well as the intermediate directions beginning with the northeast, there are, in sequence, red Bhauma riding a goat.

He holds a spear. Some say that he holds a curved knife (*chu-gri*) in his right hand and a human head in the manner of devouring it in his left. The remaining one is green and holds a bow and arrow; he stands upon a lotus and holds a yellow counting-bead rosary (*pur-bu*) and a water-pot (*ril-ba*). Some say he holds a jewel and a counting-bead rosary. He rides upon a frog. Pa-sangs is white.

The black *Po-bgraṅ-phreṅ* (Gaṇeśa) holds a rosary and a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) and stands upon a lotus. The black *Spen-pa* (Śiva) holds a rosary and a staff and rides upon a tortoise. *Sgra-gcan* (Rāhu), dark red, stands upon a chariot with the sun and moon as his seat; he has four fangs that utterly destroy the blazing, orange-red hair and beard, and his hands hold the sun and moon.

Some say that he likewise holds a *tōg* (crown) and a *dud ka* (staff), a sword and a nāga-noose, and holds the fruit of the *ātstsha bri ti* and a *kakati-tra*. Regarding the grain of rice (*ze 'bru*), there is yellow Brahmā with four faces and four arms; with his right hands he holds a rosary and displays the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya-mudrā*), while with his left hands he holds a three-pronged staff.

One should visualize all the gods dwelling there, surrounded by Brahmā holding a water-pot and riding a swan with matted hair and carrying offerings, as well as those of the Heaven of the Thirty-three, Tuṣita, and so forth, and the Retinue of Brahmā, the Ministers of Brahmā, and others.

On the eastern and other petals of the lotus situated beneath the source of phenomena (dharmodayā), there are, in sequence, Vāsuki, Śaṅkhapāla, Ananta, and Takṣaka, who are green, yellow, blue, and white respectively. On the intermediate petals in the directions of Īśāna and so forth, there are Karkoṭaka, Kulika, Mahāpadma, and...

The lotuses are red, variegated, white, and pale-white; some say they are the red Vasuki, the black Takṣaka, and the yellow Kulika. These [snakes] have seven hoods, with white tips that protrude slightly; all of them are half-human in body, wearing jeweled crowns.

One should visualize the asuras and hell-beings, complete with all their ornaments, remaining in a circle with their remains [intact], clad in armor and wielding swords. Those residing on the central, upper, and lower lotuses have completely cast off their respective forms; [they appear as] mind, body, and...

Those born from the syllables HŪṂ, OṂ, and ĀḤ, which are the nature of speech—black, white, and red in color, with one face and two arms, holding a vajra and a bell, embracing their natural consorts, and seated in the posture with the right leg extended—are consecrated by the Buddhas in the form of Heruka.

Having visualized them as being sealed by Akṣobhya, Vairocana, and Amitābha, and having consecrated the eyes and other sense organs with Mohavajrī and the others, one then [recites] without interruption: *oṃ pravara-satkāra arghaṃ pratīccha svāhā*.

Having offered the *arghya* (offering water) to them in front with the aforementioned mantra and the conch-vessel mudrā, one should offer the *pādya* (water for the feet) to their feet with the conch-vessel mudrā. Then, having summoned them with this: *inda jama jala jakkha bhūta vahni bau rakkha canda sudzja mada pappa talapātali āṭṭa sappasvāhā*.

Accompanied by graceful gestures and the sound of bells, one should consume the food of the torma—which has been transformed into nectar as before—by means of the yoga of the tongue-vajra. One should eat and drink while contemplating that those [substances] are likewise experienced in that very same way. *aiṃ dāṃ ba liṃ | bhunja | jighra | phulla | dhūppa | māṃsa | piṅga | āmbha | sapta | kaḍḍa*.

Pure and impure, *muni* *ai*; the limbs of the body, *caṇḍa* *bi*; those who are born in the world, *pāṇi* *ai*; everywhere in the world, *kuru* *phata* *ai*; the teeth are not struck, *din dimata* *hiṃ na vajra* *ai*. Afterwards, purify with incense.

Having presented the *bali* offering and performed the perfect worship, one should recite "Oṃ āḥ vajrapuṣpe hūṃ svāhā" and, having offered with incense (*dhūpa*) and so forth, recite the hundred-syllable mantra as before for the purpose of purifying any errors of omission or addition in the ritual that one has not distinguished oneself. Then, request them to depart. Furthermore, the *bali* should be recited without interruption in this sequence.

By the light rays from the syllable *hūṃ* at the heart of the form of Hevajra, there appears a vast celestial palace situated within a source of phenomena (*dharmodayā*) located at the center of the protection wheel together with the ten wrathful deities, and within that, the maṇḍala.

In the directions and so forth outside the protective wheel, the sense faculties and their retinues, as well as immeasurable sentient beings who have been summoned, are dissolved into clear light; then, one again visualizes them in the form of Heruka together with Prajñā, and performs the offering of food and so forth as before, beginning with the purification of the *bali* offering.

With the mantra: *oṃ trelokyākṣepayi maṃ baliṃ gṛhṇa gṛhṇa amukasya rakṣāṃ śāntiṃ rakṣāṃ kuru hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*, one should offer food to the Blessed One. Furthermore, with the mantras beginning with *oṃ jvala vajra* and so forth, one should give the respective pledges (*samaya*) by addressing each [deity] individually and offer food with their own individual mantras.

Having addressed [the deities] with "oṃ āḥ nairātmye āḥ" and so forth, and having recited their seed-syllables as well: "amukasya śāntiṃ rakṣāṃ kuru hūṃ svāhā | oṃ hūṃ," [one offers to] Nairātmyā and the others. Omnipresence of all phenomena! Seal of the universal assembly! Oṃ sitatapatra! Oṃ vimalā! Oṃ gṛhṇākara! Oṃ pratyamgira! Oṃ vajra-uṣṇīṣacakravarti! All mechanical devices and mantras, root activities, bonds, and those who cause harm—act for me! Whatever has been done by anyone, all of that: *tschinda tschinda*! (Cut it, cut it!)

Bhinda bhinda! Tsi ri tsi ri! Gi ri gi ri! Ma ra ma ra! Hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ! Oṃ sumbha ni sumbha hūṃ! Gṛhṇa gṛhṇa hūṃ! Gṛhṇāpaya gṛhṇāpaya hūṃ! Ānaya ho bhagavān vidyarāja hūṃ phaṭ!

With these ten mantras spoken in the *Ḍākinīvajrapañjara*, one should proceed clockwise through the directions starting from the east and so forth, as well as the intermediate directions starting from the northeast and so forth, and also toward the zenith and nadir, to the ten wrathful deities beginning with Yamāntaka. Oṃ āṃ īṃ jaḥ maṃ jaḥ laḥ.

With these and other [mantras], one should likewise offer [the nectar] to the sense faculties and so forth as before; having tasted the nectar as before, they attain supreme great bliss and, thinking, "I shall accomplish the practitioner's desired aim," they perform the aspiration prayers and so forth, and then request [the deities] to depart as before.

This is the second section on the torma ritual of the generation stage (*utpattikrama*). In the generation stage, by tasting the mere flavor of the seminal essence (*bindu*) through the movement of wisdom (*prajñā*) and method (*upāya*), one develops devotion toward those who are the very nature of wisdom and method.

Likewise, the ritual of the torma (*bali*) consists of making offerings with a torma that is inseparable from the flavor of primordial wisdom (*jñāna-rasa*) to the eyes and other faculties—such as those of the central deity of the mandala—as well as to the eyes and other faculties of one's own desired [deities], together with their benefits.

It is said that by reciting mantras with properly measured rosaries that have been prepared according to the ritual instructions, one will swiftly receive the accomplishments (*siddhi*). Therefore, I shall briefly describe those rituals: the eyes [should be fixed] upon the deity with exceptional devotion.

The method is knowledge by its very nature. Because it makes that clear, it is called "sutra" (cord); thus, *ākāśasūtra*. It is an *ākāśasūtra* because it is the cord for syllables and because it serves as a means of counting; that is, a rosary (*gaṇanāmālā*). By the rule "after *ai*, [the suffix] *ra* is not expressed," the *repha* is elided. In that regard, there are [beads of] pearls, crystal, and...

With pills made beautiful and spherical from bone and so forth, one performs pacifying activities; with silver and so forth, enriching activities; with red sandalwood, coral, and so forth, magnetizing activities; and with rudrākṣa, antelope horn, buffalo bone, and so forth, activities of wrathful sorcery.

All of this practitioner’s ritual activities are taught in the *Sampuṭatilaka*, and in the *Hevajra-tantra* (Second Part), it says: "Recitation with crystal for [achieving] paralysis; With *ni-raṃ-śu* for causing hatred; With horse bone for expelling; With Brahmin bone for summoning; And with elephant bone for bringing down rain. Furthermore, one hundred pills bring about pacification (*śāntika*), while eight more than that bring about enrichment (*pauṣṭika*).

With twenty-five [recitations], one performs subjugation; with sixty, one performs sorcery; and for all rites of enrichment, [one uses] the same number. As stated in the Mañjuśrī-tantra: "One hundred and eight, or twenty-five, fifty, or likewise fifty—the mantra practitioner who seeks the welfare of all should string these rosaries of that measure. Eight thousand [recitations] should be performed in the same way."

"The garlands are the size of a thumb; thus there are four types of garlands which the mantra-practitioner should string here. Regarding that, the cords made by young maidens represent the eight Bodhisattvas, such as Padmapāṇi and the others, who are the purity of the cardinal and intermediate directions; they are eight in number.

In the center, through the complete purity of Vajrasattva, the nature of the perfectly awakened Buddha, there is one; thus, having wound together the threads of the nine qualities, the pills are strung upon the cord in sequence. Above the two knots at the ends of the cord are the pills, which are the very Dharmakāya of the primary qualities, such as the power of universal reliance and fearlessness.
Above that, another pill is the *dharmadhātu-tathatā*.

Then, one should consecrate pills of sandalwood and so forth with colors corresponding to activities such as pacification (*śāntika*) and the rest. By reciting the mantras of Vajrasattva and others, one purifies them with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and the five lamps (*pañcapradīpa*); then, quickly visualizing the fingers of the right hand in the form of a five-pronged vajra, one should [proceed].

The sun, born from the syllable *āḥ*, consecrates that [lotus]. On the left hand, which is clearly manifest in the form of lotus petals, there is the mark of a deer produced from the complete transformation of the first vowel; it consecrates [the lotus], and one holds the counting rosary in the center of the mouth, which is the nature of wisdom (*prajñā*) and method (*upāya*).

One should meditate on the form of Hevajra as being uninterrupted, either in the nature of the desired deity or as a single whole. *Akṣarukāraṇyatu āsohi āmanta bisaru gani āsaṃkhāli sidzda ai tata tu bisaru oṃ padepade mahājñāna sarvabuddha māgrīṇadha mā haṃdha bite hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ hoṃ hoṃ hoṃ āḥ svāhā.*

Thus, one should perform the consecration; furthermore, one should also perform the consecration by reciting the mantra one hundred and eight times. This is the ritual for consecration (*pratisthā-vidhi*). Following that, with the firm conviction that the tree itself and compassion are inseparable, one should, with the right hand, [perform the rites] for the activities of pacifying (*śāntika*), enriching (*pauṣṭika*), magnetizing (*vaśya*), and forceful subjugation (*abhicāruka*).

Just as with the number [of fingers], one should place a string of medicinal herbs upon the threatening gesture (tarjanī), the middle finger, the ring finger, and the little finger. Visualizing the tip of the thumb as having the form of a stone, pebble, or iron hook, and maintaining the intention of summoning the deity, one should recite the mantra; this will bring about swift accomplishment. One must also rely upon the commitments (samaya).

"By means of practicing yoga, reciting mantras, and so forth, one will swiftly come to possess the fruit. Thus, some commitments (*samaya*) shall be stated: one must not abandon compassion for sentient beings; one must not speak of others as lacking in the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla*); one must not perform rites of sorcery (*abhicāra*); and [one must avoid] fear, despondency, and anger.

Furthermore, one should completely renounce [worldly things], not proclaiming one's own virtues for the sake of gain, honor, and the like; one should not perform mudrās, maṇḍalas, or mantras based on mere personal conceptualization; and one should understand that the various mantras spoken by the Sugata and the deities themselves are indivisible. In whatever place—

One should repeatedly practice receiving the Dharma and ritual procedures from the gurus, buddhas, bodhisattvas, and others; cultivate conviction that things such as what is edible and what is inedible are by nature completely pure; and habituate oneself to engaging in the protection of those who are harmed by the world.

Having led those who engage in evil deeds, one should cause them to attain the innermost core within oneself; and for the sake of removing the doubts of practitioners—both yogins and yoginīs—who perceive themselves as the very nature of yoga, one should cultivate familiarity with the signs that are to be seen.

Just as the five sensory qualities gathered together are to be enjoyed by the purity of the five Tathāgatas, one should not cause women to suffer, and in particular, one must not speak harsh words to the mudrā-consorts; one must not conceptualize the forms of signs or edible things, and one must abandon companions who are like thieves.

Having prepared pills from the five nectars and the five lamps on the eighth or fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should dry them in the shade, place them in a skull-cup vessel with its opening facing downward, and daily partake of them after transforming them into nectar as prescribed. Furthermore, one should strive to avoid the fourteen root downfalls and the eight gross downfalls.

Since those are already well-known, they have not been written here. Furthermore, many other various and marvelous distinctions of samaya, which were taught by the Blessed One in the tantras and elaborated upon by the accomplished ones (*siddhas*), should be understood in this way; one should not practice them nor speak of the samayas. Having observed the many varieties of skillful means and various modes of clear realization, and having also exerted effort regarding other methods of accomplishment, this has been composed by me at the request of a few earnest disciples who sought the unsurpassed Guru, who is like their very life.

Although I am like a mere reflection, whatever slight explanation of the Sage’s intention I have provided through being exhorted, that is indeed a base practice; it is accompanied by downfall and will lead to the hells. Whatever merit I have accumulated by composing this *Abhisamayatilaka*, by that may [beings] swiftly [attain] glorious Hevajra.

This *Śrī-hevajra-abhisamaya-tilaka*, composed by the renowned scholar and elder Śākyarakṣita, who became a vessel for yogins and the world, is complete. Through the grace of the glorious Byang chub rtse mo, the sovereign of scripture and reasoning and the crown jewel of those who speak two languages.

This was translated by the Śākya bhikṣu Kyobpa Palsangpo, who has attained some degree of intellectual illumination regarding the manner of symbolic conduct. From the churning of the precious source, the King of Tantras, this jewel of the two stages with white light has emerged; may it cause the *utpala* grove of those to be trained in the land of Tibet to flourish through Kyobpa Palsangpo.

By this most pure virtue arising from the translation, may all wandering beings become Vajradharas. Since I have not consulted a Paṇḍita and a second Indian manuscript was not found, may the learned forgive whatever errors there may be; let them revise it and eliminate those faulty portions.
